chapter_title: Redis Cluster: Sharding for Horizontal Scaling
chapter_summary:
While Redis replication with Sentinel provides high availability, it doesn't solve the problem of scaling beyond the capacity of a single master instance. A single master is limited by the amount of RAM it can hold and the CPU it can utilize for write operations. To overcome these limitations and achieve true horizontal scaling, Redis introduced **Redis Cluster**. Redis Cluster is a distributed implementation of Redis that automatically shards your data across multiple Redis nodes. This means your dataset is partitioned, with different parts residing on different nodes, allowing you to store much larger datasets and handle a higher throughput of operations than a single Redis instance could. Sharding is the key concept here: instead of one large database, you have several smaller, independent databases that collectively form a single logical database.

The core idea behind Redis Cluster is the concept of **hash slots**. The entire keyspace is divided into 16384 hash slots. Each key in Redis is mapped to one of these slots using a simple hashing algorithm: `CRC16(key) % 16384`. When you add a key to Redis Cluster, the cluster determines which slot it belongs to and directs the operation to the node responsible for that slot. Each node in a Redis Cluster is responsible for a subset of the 16384 hash slots. For example, Node A might handle slots 0-5000, Node B slots 5001-10000, and Node C slots 10001-16383. This distribution allows the dataset to be spread across multiple machines, overcoming the memory and CPU constraints of a single server.

A Redis Cluster is composed of multiple Redis instances, each playing a specific role. Every node in the cluster holds a portion of the hash slots and can act as a master for those slots. To ensure high availability within the cluster, each master node can have one or more replica nodes. These replicas function similarly to standalone replicas, mirroring the data of their respective masters. If a master node fails, its replicas can be promoted to take over its slots, ensuring continuous service. This means Redis Cluster combines both sharding for horizontal scaling and replication for high availability. Clients connecting to a Redis Cluster are "cluster-aware." They don't connect to a single node, but rather use a smart client library that understands the cluster's topology. When a client sends a command for a specific key, the client library calculates the hash slot for that key and directly sends the command to the correct node responsible for that slot. If the client sends a command to the wrong node, that node will respond with a `MOVED` redirection error, telling the client which node is responsible for the slot, and the client will then retry the command on the correct node.

Redis Cluster offers significant benefits for large-scale applications. It allows you to scale your Redis deployment almost linearly by adding more nodes, increasing both storage capacity and throughput. It also provides automatic failover, as replicas can take over from failed masters without manual intervention. However, it also introduces some trade-offs. The most notable limitation is that **multi-key operations are only supported if all keys involved belong to the same hash slot**. For example, `MGET` or `DEL` commands involving keys in different slots will fail. To work around this, Redis Cluster supports "hash tags," where you can force multiple keys into the same slot by enclosing a part of the key in curly braces `{}`. For example, `user:{100}:profile` and `user:{100}:cart` would both map to the same hash slot because the hash is computed only on `{100}`. This allows you to perform multi-key operations on related data.

Another important aspect is that Redis Cluster does not support certain commands or features that rely on a global view of the dataset, such as `KEYS` (which iterates over all keys in the entire cluster) or `SELECT` (which switches databases, as Redis Cluster only supports database 0). For safety, when designing your data model for Redis Cluster, always consider how your keys will be distributed and whether your application requires multi-key operations across different slots. If your application heavily relies on such operations for unrelated keys, Redis Cluster might not be the most suitable solution, and you might need to rethink your data partitioning strategy or consider alternative scaling approaches. Understanding these limitations upfront is crucial for a successful Redis Cluster deployment.

screens.title: Redis Cluster — Sharding for Horizontal Scaling
screens.subtitle: How Redis partitions data across nodes using hash slots to scale beyond a single server

narration.text: Today we will explore why Redis Cluster matters when your dataset grows beyond a single server. Replication with Sentinel gives high availability, but it doesn’t let you exceed one master's memory and C P U limits. Redis Cluster solves that by sharding: splitting the keyspace into 16,384 hash slots and distributing those slots across multiple nodes. You will learn how keys map to slots using a deterministic hash, how nodes own ranges of slots, and how replicas provide failover for each shard. We’ll also cover practical limitations, such as multi-key operations that only work when keys share the same slot, and the hash tag technique that forces related keys into one slot. By the end of this lesson, you’ll understand the cluster’s core building blocks, how cluster-aware clients route commands, and the trade-offs you accept when moving from a single master to a sharded architecture. This matters because correct partitioning and client behavior determine performance, operational complexity, and whether your application patterns are compatible with Redis Cluster.

screens.title: Why sharding is necessary
screens.subtitle: From single-master limits to many smaller shards

narration.text: Start by understanding the problem that sharding solves. A single Redis master is limited by the server's memory and C P U for writes. When your dataset grows beyond that server’s R A M, or you need much higher write throughput, a single node becomes the bottleneck. Sharding is the act of partitioning the dataset into smaller pieces, so each Redis node holds only a portion of the total keys and values. This reduces per-node memory pressure and spreads write load across multiple machines, allowing near-linear increases in capacity as you add nodes. A common misconception is that replication alone scales capacity. Replicas copy the same dataset and therefore do not increase total storage or write throughput; they only provide redundancy and read-scaling. Sharding, in contrast, increases total storage because each shard holds a different subset of the data. For example, if you split a dataset across three masters, each master stores roughly a third of the keys, so combined they hold the full dataset. Remember that sharded designs require a strategy to route requests to the right shard and a plan for what happens when a shard fails. Consider how data-level relationships and multi-key operations will work in a partitioned topology before adopting sharding.

keyIdea.title: Sharding defined
keyIdea.text: Sharding partitions a large dataset into smaller subsets across multiple nodes, enabling more memory and write capacity than a single server can provide.

content.html:
Core Concept
Why sharding is necessary
Partitioning the keyspace so Redis can scale horizontally.
Definition
Sharding splits a dataset into independent pieces so multiple servers together host a single logical database.
  • • Shards reduce per-node memory and CPU usage.
  • • Replication copies data but does not add capacity.
  • • Sharding requires predictable routing to the correct shard.
Key Takeaway

Sharding increases total storage and write capacity by distributing different keys to different nodes, unlike replication which duplicates the same dataset.

Analogy & Example
Think of a library divided into sections by topic instead of one giant hall.
If one hall runs out of space, splitting books into sections lets you add rooms rather than expand a single room. Similarly, three Redis masters can collectively hold a dataset too large for one master.
Shard A: keys 0—4999
Shard B: keys 5000—9999
Shard C: keys 10000—16383
Common mistake: assuming replicas will scale writes or storage. They only protect and can serve reads; sharding is required to expand the working dataset.

screens.title: What is Redis Cluster?
screens.subtitle: A distributed Redis that shards data and uses replicas for availability

narration.text: Redis Cluster is Redis implemented as a distributed system that shards data across multiple Redis instances and pairs sharding with replication for availability. Each master node owns a set of hash slots and can have one or more replicas. Those replicas continuously mirror the master’s assigned data so they are ready to take over if the master fails. Importantly, the cluster is not a single monolithic server; it is a collection of cooperating instances that together present a logical Redis deployment. Clients connecting to a Redis Cluster are cluster-aware: they calculate which slot a key belongs to and communicate directly with the node that owns that slot. If a client sends a command to the wrong node, that node returns a MOVED response, pointing the client to the correct node. This design avoids a central coordinator for most operations and lets the cluster scale horizontally by adding more master nodes. The practical effect is you get both sharding and automatic failover, but you also accept operational complexity: slot rebalancing when adding or removing nodes, and careful data-model considerations for multi-key commands.

keyIdea.title: Redis Cluster in one line
keyIdea.text: A set of Redis instances that partition the keyspace with hash slots and use replication per shard to provide availability.

content.html:
Definition
What is Redis Cluster?
Distributed sharding plus per-shard replication for availability and scaling.
Cluster components
  • • Masters: own one or more hash slot ranges and serve writes for those slots.
  • • Replicas: mirror a master’s data and can be promoted if the master fails.
  • • Cluster-aware clients: compute the key’s slot and send commands to the correct node.
Cluster combines sharding and replication: each shard is a master with its own replica set, so failure of one master affects only its slots, not the whole dataset.
Operational notes
Adding or removing nodes requires moving slot ownership and migrating data. Clients should handle MOVED redirections during topology changes. Because nodes own ranges of slots, many operations are local to a node if the key’s slot is known.
Example: Master A owns slots 0–5000, Master B 5001–10000, Master C 10001–16383
Key Takeaway

Redis Cluster is a sharded Redis with per-shard replication, enabling larger datasets and fault recovery per shard rather than cluster-wide downtime.

screens.title: Hash slots and key mapping
screens.subtitle: How keys deterministically map to one of 16,384 slots

narration.text: At the heart of Redis Cluster is the hash slot model. The entire keyspace is split into exactly 16,384 logical hash slots. When you store or fetch a key, Redis computes CRC16 of the key and takes that value modulo 16384 to produce the slot number. The formula can be expressed as CRC16(key) modulo 16384. This deterministic mapping guarantees that the same key always maps to the same slot, so the cluster knows which node must contain that key. Nodes are assigned subsets of slots; a node might own a contiguous range or multiple ranges depending on cluster layout. Knowing this, a cluster-aware client can compute the slot for a key and send commands directly to the responsible node without needing a central directory. A common misunderstanding is assuming hashing distributes keys evenly regardless of key naming patterns. Key design still matters: if many keys share a common pattern that yields similar hash outputs, one node could become a hotspot. Use key naming that spreads entropy across the full key string to support even distribution. The deterministic slot mapping is essential for predictable routing and for implementing hash tags when multi-key operations are needed.

keyIdea.title: Mapping formula
keyIdea.text: Each key maps to slot = CRC16(key) % 16384, producing a deterministic slot that indicates which node stores the key.

content.html:
Process Flow
Hash slots and key mapping
Deterministic formula that routes keys to nodes.
The mapping rule
CRC16(key) % 16384
This computation yields a number between 0 and 16383. Clients and nodes use that slot number to determine ownership. The deterministic nature means the same key always hashes to the same slot until slot ownership changes in the cluster.
Misconception: hashing instantly balances load for any key naming. In practice, choose key names with sufficient entropy across the full string to avoid hotspots.
What clients do
  • • Compute slot from the key using the CRC16 formula.
  • • Send the command directly to the node that owns that slot.
  • • If they receive MOVED, update topology and retry on the correct node.
Key Takeaway

The CRC16 modulo 16384 mapping makes slot assignment deterministic, enabling direct routing and predictable partitioning of keys across the cluster.

screens.title: Slot ownership and distribution example
screens.subtitle: How a cluster assigns slot ranges to nodes

narration.text: Let's walk through a simple distribution example to make slot ownership concrete. Imagine a small cluster with three master nodes. The cluster assigns contiguous slot ranges so Node A owns slots 0–5000, Node B owns slots 5001–10000, and Node C owns slots 10001–16383. Each node is responsible for operations whose keys map into its ranges. When you add a fourth master, the cluster can rebalance by moving some slot ranges from existing masters to the new node, migrating keys accordingly. Rebalancing must copy or move key contents between nodes so the new owner can serve requests. During migration, cluster-aware clients may see MOVED responses if a key’s slot has been reassigned; well-behaved clients follow those redirects and continue operations. A common operational pitfall is assuming slot ranges are always equal; real clusters may assign uneven ranges initially or after manual reconfiguration. Also, slot movement carries network and C P U cost, so plan capacity and growth steps to avoid frequent rebalancing. This example clarifies how ownership maps to physical nodes and why topology changes must be handled carefully. Slot ownership and distribution example means nodes claim subsets of the 16384 slots; rebalancing moves slot ownership and requires data migration between nodes.. In practical terms, how a cluster assigns slot ranges to nodes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Node roles: master and replica
screens.subtitle: How replication supports availability within each shard

narration.text: Each shard in a Redis Cluster has a master node that owns specific hash slots and one or more replicas that mirror the master's data. Replicas are not used to increase total storage; instead, they provide high availability for a master’s assigned slots. If a master fails, the cluster can promote one of its replicas to become the new master for those slots. This automatic failover keeps the shard available without manual intervention. It’s important to understand that replicas only mirror their master's portion of the data — they do not hold additional, different data that extends cluster capacity. Administrators must plan replica placement for fault tolerance: place replicas on different physical hosts or racks to avoid correlated failures. A common misconception is treating replicas as a way to scale writes; they cannot accept writes that would conflict with the master without special configuration. When a master fails and a replica is promoted, clients may observe a short window of redirection or transient errors while topology information updates. Design your monitoring and operational playbooks to handle promotions and to rebalance replicas when necessary.

keyIdea.title: Master and replica roles
keyIdea.text: Masters own slots and serve writes; replicas mirror a master's slots and can be promoted to maintain availability if a master fails.

content.html:
Core Concept
Node roles: master and replica
Replication per shard provides failover without increasing shard capacity.
Master
Owns specific hash slots and accepts writes for those slots. Its replicas replicate the same subset of keys to enable failover.
Replica
Continuously mirrors a master's data. If the master fails, a replica can be promoted to master for that shard.
Operational guidance
  • • Place replicas on separate hosts or racks to avoid correlated outages.
  • • Replicas do not add writable capacity for that shard; writes must go to the master.
  • • Plan for failover windows where clients receive redirections or transient errors while topology updates.
Key Takeaway

Replication in Cluster protects each shard by providing replicas that can be promoted, but replicas do not increase total shard storage or write throughput.

screens.title: Cluster-aware clients and MOVED
screens.subtitle: How clients compute a slot and what MOVED redirection means

narration.text: Client behavior is central to Redis Cluster performance. A cluster-aware client computes the target slot for a key before issuing a command, typically using the CRC16 modulo 16384 rule, and connects directly to the node owning that slot. This direct routing minimizes hops and latency. If a client sends a command to a node that does not own the slot, the node responds with a MOVED redirection containing the address of the correct node. Well-implemented clients follow the MOVED reply, update their internal view of the cluster topology, and retry the command on the indicated node. A common error is using a client that is not cluster-aware; such clients rely on an intermediary and can introduce extra latency or fail under reconfiguration. Another important note is that during slot migration — when ownership is changing — clients may see MOVED responses temporarily until migration completes and topology stabilizes. Building robust clients includes handling redirections smoothly and refreshing slot data occasionally to avoid stale routing information. This behavior keeps the cluster consistent without a centralized router and enables scalability. Cluster-aware clients and MOVED means clients compute slots and send commands to the node that owns them; moved responses inform the client to retry on the correct node and refresh topology.. In practical terms, how clients compute a slot and what moved redirection means. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Client routing
keyIdea.text: Clients compute slots and send commands to the node that owns them; MOVED responses inform the client to retry on the correct node and refresh topology.

content.html:
Process Flow
Cluster-aware clients and MOVED
How clients compute a slot and handle redirection responses during normal operations and topology changes.
Client steps
  1. Compute slot = CRC16(key) % 16384.
  2. Send command directly to the node owning that slot.
  3. If node replies MOVED, update topology and retry on the indicated node.
Misconception: MOVED is an error you must fix manually. In fact, cluster-aware clients handle it automatically and use it to correct routing information.
Practical example
If your client sends SET user:100:name to Node X but slot 123 maps to Node Y, Node X replies MOVED with Node Y’s address. The client then retries on Node Y. If the cluster is migrating slots, MOVED responses help the client land on the authoritative node while migration proceeds.
Pro tip

Use a maintained, cluster-aware client library rather than building routing logic yourself to avoid common pitfalls and stale topology caches.

screens.title: Multi-key operations and slot constraints
screens.subtitle: Why multi-key commands only work when keys share a slot

narration.text: One of the most important limitations in Redis Cluster is how multi-key operations are handled. Commands that operate on multiple keys, like MGET or DEL, require that all involved keys map to the same hash slot. If the keys belong to different slots, the operation will fail. This restriction exists because multi-key commands must be executed atomically on a single node; if keys are spread across nodes, the cluster cannot guarantee atomicity or consistent ordering without a central coordinator. A common misconception is that the cluster transparently coordinates multi-key operations across nodes. It does not. To enable multi-key operations on related keys, Redis provides hash tags: by enclosing a substring in curly braces, the client forces the hash calculation to consider only that substring. For example, user:{100}:profile and user:{100}:cart both hash the inner 100 and therefore map to the same slot. This technique lets you design related keys so multi-key commands work. However, overusing hash tags can lead to uneven distribution if too many keys use the same tag. Balance the need for atomic multi-key operations against even data distribution when you design key patterns.

keyIdea.title: Multi-key rule
keyIdea.text: Multi-key commands must reference keys in the same slot; use hash tags to force related keys into one slot for atomic operations.

content.html:
Comparison
Multi-key operations and slot constraints
Compare single-key semantics with multi-key restrictions in a cluster.
Single-key commands
Operate on one key and route directly to the owner of that slot. These commands are straightforward in Cluster because the server owning the slot executes them locally.
Examples: GET, SET — work normally because only one slot is involved.
Multi-key commands
Require all keys to belong to the same slot. If they don’t, the command fails to avoid cross-node atomicity and ordering issues.
Examples: MGET key1 key2 — succeeds only if key1 and key2 map to the same slot.
Design implication: use hash tags like {id} to group related keys when you need multi-key operations. But avoid funneling all keys through a single tag unless necessary, as that creates hotspots.

screens.title: Hash tags: forcing keys into the same slot
screens.subtitle: How { ... } controls what part of the key is hashed

narration.text: Hash tags let you force multiple keys to map to the same hash slot by defining an explicit substring for the hashing algorithm. When Redis sees a key containing a substring in curly braces, it computes the hash only over the characters inside the braces. For instance, the keys user:{100}:profile and user:{100}:cart both hash the inner 100 and therefore map to the same slot, enabling multi-key commands like MGET or transactions across those keys. Use this feature to co-locate related data that must be accessed together atomically. Remember, hash tags change how keys distribute across the cluster — forcing many keys to share the same tag concentrates load on a single slot and its owning node, which can become a hotspot. A typical pattern is to use an identifier that groups related records, such as a user id or order id, only when you truly need grouped multi-key operations. Also be deliberate about your tag placement to ensure predictable hashing. Hash tags do not change replica or failover behavior; they only affect which slot a key maps to within the existing slot ownership layout.

keyIdea.title: Hash tag rule
keyIdea.text: Anything inside curly braces is the only portion hashed; use it to ensure related keys land in the same slot for multi-key operations.

content.html:
Definition
Hash tags: forcing keys into the same slot
Curly braces let you pick which substring is hashed for slot assignment.
How it works
user:{100}:profile
user:{100}:cart
order:{ABC}:items
order:{ABC}:details
Keys that share the same inner braces content hash to the same slot and can be used together in multi-key commands.
Design guidance
  • • Use tags for related records that require multi-key operations.
  • • Avoid overusing the same tag value across large datasets to prevent hotspots.
  • • Tags do not change replication or failover behavior, only slot mapping.
Key Takeaway

Hash tags let related keys be co-located in one slot so multi-key operations succeed; use them judiciously to avoid creating hotspots.

screens.title: Unsupported commands and single-database model
screens.subtitle: Commands that rely on a global dataset view are not available in Cluster

narration.text: Redis Cluster intentionally restricts some commands that need a global view of all keys. Commands like KEYS, which iterates all keys in the database, are not supported because keys live on different nodes and iterating them cluster-wide would be complex and unsafe. Similarly, Redis Cluster only supports database 0 and does not implement SELECT to switch logical databases. Those features rely on a centralized dataset or multiple databases on a single server—models that conflict with sharding. When designing for Cluster, avoid patterns that require listing or scanning all keys from a single node. Instead use application-level indexes or maintain your own metadata keys placed intentionally with hash tags if you need rapid group lookups. A common misconception is that Cluster removes the need for careful data modeling; in fact it increases the need to plan key layout and access patterns. If your application relies heavily on scanning across all keys or using multiple logical databases, Cluster may be a poor fit without redesigning how you locate and group data across shards. Unsupported commands and single-database model means cluster does not support global commands like keys or database switching with select; design your model without relying on cluster-wide scans or multiple databases.. In practical terms, commands that rely on a global dataset view are not available in cluster. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Global commands
keyIdea.text: Cluster does not support global commands like KEYS or database switching with SELECT; design your model without relying on cluster-wide scans or multiple databases.

content.html:
Definition
Unsupported commands and single-database model
Cluster avoids commands that require a global dataset view.
Not supported
  • • KEYS — not supported cluster-wide because keys live on different nodes.
  • • SELECT — Cluster only uses database 0; multiple logical DBs aren’t supported.
Design alternatives
Maintain application-level indexes or metadata keys co-located with hash tags for group lookups. Replace global scans with targeted queries and careful key modeling.
Common mistake

Trying to run KEYS on a single node will produce incomplete results because other nodes own other slots.

screens.title: Benefits and trade-offs compared to Sentinel
screens.subtitle: When to use Cluster versus master-replica with Sentinel

narration.text: Comparing Redis Cluster to a master-replica setup managed by Sentinel helps you choose the right approach. With Sentinel and a single master, you get high availability through failover, and replicas can serve reads, but all data still resides on one master for writes and storage. This design simplifies multi-key operations and global commands because the dataset is local to one server. Redis Cluster, by contrast, shards data across multiple masters so total capacity and write throughput increase as you add shards. Cluster also provides automatic failover for each shard through replicas. The trade-offs are clear: Cluster increases horizontal capacity and throughput but restricts multi-key operations across slots and disallows global commands like KEYS. Sentinel setups keep full single-node semantics but cannot scale beyond the master’s hardware limits. Choose Cluster when you must grow beyond a single server and can design keys accordingly. Choose Sentinel when your application depends heavily on global operations or multi-key commands across unrelated keys and you cannot refactor the data model. Benefits and trade-offs compared to Sentinel means sentinel preserves single-node semantics but doesn’t increase capacity; cluster scales capacity and throughput but imposes multi-key and global command constraints.. In practical terms, when to use cluster versus master-replica with sentinel. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trade-off summary
keyIdea.text: Sentinel preserves single-node semantics but doesn’t increase capacity; Cluster scales capacity and throughput but imposes multi-key and global command constraints.

content.html:
Comparison
Benefits and trade-offs compared to Sentinel
Pick the deployment pattern that matches capacity and data-model needs.
Master-replica + Sentinel
  • • Simpler semantics: single master holds full dataset.
  • • Supports global commands and multi-key ops across the dataset.
  • • Limited by single server memory and write capacity.
Redis Cluster
  • • Shards data across nodes for larger storage and higher write throughput.
  • • Provides per-shard replication and automatic failover.
  • • Restricts multi-key ops across slots and disallows certain global commands.
Key Takeaway

Choose Sentinel if your workload needs global operations and you cannot shard; choose Cluster to scale capacity and writes, and design keys around slot rules.

screens.title: Design guidance and limitations
screens.subtitle: Model keys, plan for rebalancing, and avoid unsupported patterns

narration.text: When designing for Redis Cluster, follow a few practical rules. First, model keys so that related data you need to operate on together either naturally maps to the same slot or uses hash tags intentionally. Second, avoid patterns that require cluster-wide scans or multiple logical databases, because Cluster does not support KEYS or SELECT. Third, plan cluster growth in coarse steps to minimize frequent slot migrations; each migration copies or moves keys and carries network and C P U cost. Fourth, place replicas to avoid correlated failure by using different physical hosts or availability zones. Common limitations include the inability to perform multi-key operations across slots and the lack of global commands; if your application depends on those operations for unrelated keys, you may need to reconsider using Cluster or refactor the application logic. For example, maintain an application index table or use a single-shard design for the dataset portion that requires global operations. Finally, test client behavior during topology changes so your clients correctly handle MOVED responses and temporary redirections. Good planning reduces surprises when operating a cluster in production.

keyIdea.title: Design checklist
keyIdea.text: Model keys with slot behavior in mind, avoid global scans, plan rebalancing, and place replicas for fault isolation to operate Cluster safely.

content.html:
Process Flow
Design guidance and limitations
Practical checklist for building cluster-ready applications.
Model keys
Use hash tags for related keys and ensure enough entropy in key naming to avoid hotspots.
Avoid global scans
Replace KEYS with application-level indexes or targeted queries co-located with relevant data.
Plan rebalancing
Grow clusters in planned steps; each slot move transfers data and impacts resources.
Common mistake

Assuming Cluster removes the need to design keys carefully. In reality, careful key design is essential to avoid hotspots and operation failures.

Operational tip

Test client behavior during topology changes so MOVED redirections are handled smoothly and your app remains resilient.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let’s summarize the essential concepts. Sharding partitions a dataset into shards so multiple masters can hold different parts of the data, enabling horizontal scaling. Redis Cluster implements sharding using 16,384 hash slots, with a deterministic mapping computed by CRC16(key) modulo 16384. Nodes claim subsets of those slots, and each master can have replicas that mirror its slots for failover. Cluster-aware clients compute slots and send commands to the node owning the slot; if a command reaches the wrong node, the server replies with a MOVED redirection that tells the client where to retry. Multi-key commands only work when all keys map to the same slot; hash tags in curly braces let you force co-location of related keys to enable these operations. Finally, Cluster does not support global commands like KEYS or multiple databases with SELECT, so design your data model accordingly. These are the building blocks that will guide choices when scaling Redis and designing keys for predictable distribution.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Sharding via 16,384 slots, cluster-aware clients, replicas per shard, and hash tags for multi-key needs are the core takeaways.

content.html:
What to Remember
Key Concepts
Three compact concept cards and a summary takeaway.
Sharding
Partitioning the dataset across multiple nodes to increase total storage and throughput.
Hash Slots
16,384 logical slots map keys to nodes using CRC16(key) modulo 16384.
Hash Tags
Use curly braces to force multiple keys to the same slot for multi-key operations.
Summary

Redis Cluster shards data across 16,384 slots with per-shard replication for availability. Clients must be cluster-aware and keys must be modeled to respect slot constraints when multi-key operations are required.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three concise reminders for practical use

narration.text: To close, remember three practical rules: one, treat replicas as availability mechanisms, not extra capacity — they mirror a master’s assigned slots. Two, always use a cluster-aware client that computes slots and follows MOVED redirections automatically. Three, design your keys consciously: use hash tags only when you need multi-key atomicity, and avoid global scans by using application-level indexes. These simple habits make Redis Cluster predictable and reliable as you scale. If you can’t conform your application to these constraints, re-evaluate whether Cluster is the right fit or consider hybrid approaches for parts of the system that require global operations. Final Notes
What to Remember
Three concise reminders for operating Redis Cluster effectively.
Replicas
Provide failover for a shard; they do not increase writable capacity of the cluster.
Clients
Must be cluster-aware to compute slots and follow MOVED responses for correct routing.
Key design
Use hash tags to co-locate related keys and avoid global commands by maintaining targeted indexes.
Final takeaway

Redis Cluster lets you scale horizontally but requires deliberate client and key design. Apply these reminders to avoid common pitfalls during scaling and operations.
